column3: The Hebrew asks “What is my sin before your father?” and says he seeks David’s soul. BSB makes the question verbal, “How have I sinned,” and renders seeking the soul as wanting to take his life.
The Hebrew leaves the speaker unnamed and describes disclosure as uncovering his ear. BSB supplies Jonathan and uses “telling me.”
The Hebrew’s oath explicitly invokes “your soul” living; BSB renders this as “you yourself” living.
The Hebrew asks what David’s “soul says”; BSB renders this as “Whatever you desire.”
The Hebrew explicitly names Jonathan as recipient and repeats the sitting root in the expected meal. BSB uses “him” and renders the expectation as “I am supposed to dine.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew says there is “peace for your servant”; BSB says “your servant is safe.” It describes evil as determined by the father, rendered “he has evil intentions.”
The Hebrew repeats “your servant” and calls the agreement “a covenant of the LORD”; BSB uses “me” and “a covenant with you before the LORD.”
Close to the Hebrew.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew explicitly names Jonathan speaking to David; BSB uses “he replied.”
The Hebrew names David as the one toward whom the father may be favorable; BSB uses “you.” Its disclosure image is uncovering the ear, rendered “tell you.”
The Hebrew’s oath names Jonathan, where BSB uses “me.” It says to uncover David’s ear and send him in peace; BSB uses telling him and sending him “in safety.”
Close to the Hebrew.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew’s accountability expression is seeking “from the hand of David’s enemies”; BSB leaves the hand image implicit in holding them accountable.
The Hebrew leaves the loving subjects and objects as pronouns and explicitly names love of his soul. BSB supplies Jonathan and David and renders the soul as “himself.”
The Hebrew pairs two forms of the same missing or attending root; BSB uses “be missed” and “is empty.”
The Hebrew calls the earlier occasion “the day of the deed”; BSB specifies “the day this trouble began.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew says “there is no matter” against David; BSB specifies “there is no danger.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew says the LORD is between them forever; BSB supplies “a witness.”
The Hebrew explicitly says the king sat to the bread to eat; BSB leaves the bread implicit.
The Hebrew says Jonathan rose and Abner sat beside Saul; BSB instead describes the king sitting opposite Jonathan and beside Abner.
The Hebrew leaves David unnamed and has no separate term corresponding to “ceremonially”; BSB supplies both.
The Hebrew again calls the meal “the bread”; BSB uses “the meal.”
The Hebrew explicitly names Saul as the recipient of the answer; BSB leaves him implicit.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew’s final shame expression explicitly refers to “the nakedness of your mother”; BSB instead says “the mother who bore you.”
